summary:
Central Java is a province of Indonesia, and a visitor there stands under Indonesia's national legal framework. The sources record no criminalisation of gender identity itself, no X marker on identity documents, and no legal recognition of same-sex marriage, and they document no Central Java provision that would alter that position for a visitor.

The national penal code was passed by the House of Representatives on 6 December 2022, signed by President Joko Widodo, and took effect on 2 January 2026, three years after enactment. It criminalises sexual activity outside marriage, with penalties reported at up to two years' imprisonment under the framework and at up to one year where a complaint is lodged by an immediate family member. The code does not explicitly criminalise same-sex relationships, but because Indonesia does not recognise same-sex marriage, all sexual activity between same-sex couples falls within the outside-marriage restriction. Reporting indicates prosecutions are selective rather than systematic. The code drew international criticism, including from the United Nations, for failing to accommodate protections and rights for LGBT individuals and domestic partnerships.

Indonesia recognises only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors, with no third-gender or X option. Since June 2021 the Ministry of Home Affairs has run outreach issuing transgender Indonesians identification papers (KTP), printing birth-gender unless a court order was already obtained; electronic ID cards were issued to transgender people in nine provinces. Legal gender recognition requires sex reassignment surgery and a judge's approval. No national law protects people from discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity.

Physical risk is rising across the country. An August 2026 feature records growing repression of Indonesia's transgender community, and reporting ties a surge in vigilante mob attacks on transgender people to officials' public condemnations and to a presidential decree of October 2025 listing LGBTQ+ people as a non-military national threat alongside separatism and terrorism. Police raids on LGBT gatherings continue; on 22 June 2025 officers raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor and arrested 75 people, and Amnesty International said the gathering violated no law. Transgender identity (waria) has long been part of Indonesian culture, alongside documented repressive incidents including raids on transgender women by the Jakarta Social Agency.

Expression is criminalised in ways a visitor can trigger. The 2006 Law Against Pornography and Pornoaction punishes any writing or audio-visual presentation showing or suggesting same-sex relations with up to seven years' imprisonment, and the government has blocked websites and apps carrying LGBTQ-related words. Aceh and South Sumatra additionally criminalise same-sex sexual activity under provincial provisions that apply to anyone present in those provinces, not to visitors in Central Java.
tangentialFactors:
Custody has proved lethal for a trans traveller: in August 2022 Rodrigo Ventocilla, a Harvard student on honeymoon in Bali, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges and died in custody, with his mother alleging police beat him and Indonesian police denying that violence was used.

Two provinces outside Central Java, Aceh and South Sumatra, criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women; Aceh's punishments are imposed under provincial religious law and apply to anyone present in that province. In Aceh two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025, and two men were flogged in January 2021. These provisions do not reach a visitor who remains in Central Java.

Indonesia's position differs from neighbouring jurisdictions in that gender identity itself is not criminalised, while sexual activity outside marriage is restricted for everyone regardless of orientation.

outOfScopeNotes:
The sources do not document any Central Java-specific provincial regulation on gender identity, same-sex relations, or facilities that would differ from the national framework; whether such a local bylaw exists is unresolved and not sourced here.

The sources do not resolve how selectively the outside-marital-sex provision of the 2022 penal code is enforced in Central Java specifically; reporting characterises prosecutions nationally as selective rather than systematic.

Whether Central Java has any provincial-level response to the October 2025 presidential decree listing LGBTQ+ people as a non-military national threat is not sourced.
